steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our journal extension of a paper on automatically tagging issues with API-domain labels in issue trackers. Explain the problem for OSS newcomers, the idea of API-domain labels, what this extension adds over the earlier case study, the research questions, and the contributions.

- Idea: APIs as indicators of skills; API-domain labels
- Extension of prior work: why and what is added

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
It can be hard to choose a task to contribute to in Open Source Software (OSS) projects. Open tasks are reported publicly in issue trackers, but issues are different in complexity and in the skills they require, so contributors may find it hard to pick a task that suits them, especially if they are new in the project. Adding labels to issues (also called “tasks,” “tickets,” and “bug reports”) is an effective way to help new contributors decide where to focus their efforts. The labeling strategy helps many kinds of contributors, including newcomers (new contributors), frequent contributors and maintainers, since they have similar perceptions of how important this strategy is. Developers are newcomers every time they start a new project, no matter how much experience they have. But community managers and project maintainers find it challenging and time-consuming to label issues manually.

Our idea is that the underlying APIs (the libraries required and imported into the source code) can be parsed to show the skills needed to work on an issue. APIs are defined as “a set of functions and procedures that enable the creation of applications that access the resources or data of an operating system, application or other services”. If contributors know what types of APIs are used in the code that solves the issue, they could choose tasks that match their skills better or that involve skills they want to learn. We use the idea that APIs encapsulate modules with specific purposes (e.g., cryptography, database access, logging) and hide the implementation details. In this study we focus on API-domain labels, which are high-level labels for categories of APIs such as “UI,” “Security,” and “Test,” and which may relate to the skills needed to work on the issues.

This paper extends our prior work, where we did a case study with one project to see if it was feasible to label issues automatically with API-domain labels. When we ran the first predictions in the case study, we saw that the number of dataset rows dropped a lot because there was no information about linked issues and PRs. Because of this, and to generalize better, we looked for ways to increase the datasets when a project is seriously affected by dataset size after the issues not linked with a PR are discarded. Also, in industry projects it is sometimes impossible to access the source because of confidentiality. So we looked for ways to keep predicting the API-domain labels even without training data, by transferring the learning. We think the API-domain labels would be even more helpful if they can be used in many open-source or industry projects regardless of the dataset size or availability of their source code. We extend the work by (1) expanding the study to five projects with different programming languages, vocabularies (natural languages), and issue track systems (ITS), (2) adding the BERT technique to the approach, (3) extending the qualitative analysis, (4) exploring if learning can be transferred across projects, and (5) evaluating the API-domain labels with the developers who solved the issues.

- RQs
  - RQ.1 relevance to new contributors
  - RQ.2 automatic attribution; RQ.2.1 project data; RQ.2.2 other projects' data; RQ.2.3 transfer learning
  - RQ.3 match with skills needed
- How studied
  - RQ.1 relevance; models created + evaluated
  - RQ.2.1 same project train/test; RQ.2.2 enlarge with other projects; RQ.2.3 no historical data -> pre-trained dataset from same-domain source project
  - RQ.3 developers' opinions on predictions
- Contributions: (1) newcomers' view of relevance; (2) semi-automated API classification; (3) skill prediction for C, C#, Java projects, issues in Portuguese and English; (4) validation with developers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
It can be hard to choose a task to contribute to in Open Source Software (OSS) projects. Open tasks are reported publicly in issue trackers, but issues are different in complexity and in the skills they require, so contributors may find it hard to pick a task that suits them, especially if they are new in the project. Adding labels to issues (also called “tasks,” “tickets,” and “bug reports”) is an effective way to help new contributors decide where to focus their efforts. The labeling strategy helps many kinds of contributors, including newcomers (new contributors), frequent contributors and maintainers, since they have similar perceptions of how important this strategy is. Developers are newcomers every time they start a new project, no matter how much experience they have. But community managers and project maintainers find it challenging and time-consuming to label issues manually.

Our idea is that the underlying APIs (the libraries required and imported into the source code) can be parsed to show the skills needed to work on an issue. APIs are defined as “a set of functions and procedures that enable the creation of applications that access the resources or data of an operating system, application or other services”. If contributors know what types of APIs are used in the code that solves the issue, they could choose tasks that match their skills better or that involve skills they want to learn. We use the idea that APIs encapsulate modules with specific purposes (e.g., cryptography, database access, logging) and hide the implementation details. In this study we focus on API-domain labels, which are high-level labels for categories of APIs such as “UI,” “Security,” and “Test,” and which may relate to the skills needed to work on the issues.

This paper extends our prior work, where we did a case study with one project to see if it was feasible to label issues automatically with API-domain labels. When we ran the first predictions in the case study, we saw that the number of dataset rows dropped a lot because there was no information about linked issues and PRs. Because of this, and to generalize better, we looked for ways to increase the datasets when a project is seriously affected by dataset size after the issues not linked with a PR are discarded. Also, in industry projects it is sometimes impossible to access the source because of confidentiality. So we looked for ways to keep predicting the API-domain labels even without training data, by transferring the learning. We think the API-domain labels would be even more helpful if they can be used in many open-source or industry projects regardless of the dataset size or availability of their source code. We extend the work by (1) expanding the study to five projects with different programming languages, vocabularies (natural languages), and issue track systems (ITS), (2) adding the BERT technique to the approach, (3) extending the qualitative analysis, (4) exploring if learning can be transferred across projects, and (5) evaluating the API-domain labels with the developers who solved the issues.

We answer these research questions:

RQ.1: How relevant are the API-domain labels to new contributors? RQ.2: To what extent can we automatically attribute API-domain labels to issues? RQ.2.1: To what extent can we automatically attribute API-domain labels to issues using data from the project? RQ.2.2: To what extent can we automatically attribute API-domain labels to issues using data from other projects? RQ.2.3: To what extent can we automatically attribute API-domain labels to issues using transfer learning? RQ.3: How well do the API-domain labels match the skills needed to solve an issue?

We study how relevant this labeling strategy is to new contributors (RQ.1). We built models and evaluated how well they perform. Normally machine learning approaches train and test with data from the same project (RQ.2.1). But if there is not enough data to build a prediction model with the expected performance, the dataset can be enlarged with other projects (RQ.2.2). And if there is no historical data at all for training in a target project, a pre-trained dataset in the same domain (source project) can be used to run predictions in the target project (RQ.2.3). So we also did transfer learning studies. Finally, we studied what developers think about the predictions, to see if the API-domain labels indicate skills well enough and help newcomers choose their tasks (RQ.3).

Our contributions are (1) how newcomers see the relevance of the API-domain labels; (2) a new semi-automated API classification process; (3) a mechanism to predict the skills needed for projects coded in different programming languages (C, C#, and Java), with issues in Portuguese and English; and (4) the validation of the API-domain labels with developers.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Choosing a task to contribute to in Open Source Software (OSS) projects can be challenging [1,2,3,4,5]. Open tasks are publicly reported in issue trackers, but since issues vary in complexity and required skills, contributors may find it difficult to select an appropriate task to undertake, especially when they are new to the project [6,7,8,9]. Adding labels to the issues (a.k.a. “tasks,” “tickets,” and “bug reports”) is an effective way to help new contributors choose where to focus their efforts [10]. The labeling strategy supports a variety of contributors, including newcomers (new contributors), frequent contributors, and maintainers, as they have similar perceptions of its importance [11]. Developers are newcomers each time they start a new project, no matter their previous experience. Nevertheless, community managers and project maintainers find manually labeling issues challenging and time-consuming [12].

We posit that the underlying APIs (the libraries required and imported into the source code) can be parsed to indicate the skills required to work on an issue. APIs are defined as “a set of functions and procedures that enable the creation of applications that access the resources or data of an operating system, application or other services” [13]. If contributors know what types of APIs are used in the code to solve the issue, they could choose tasks that better match their skills or involve skills they want to learn. We leverage the idea that APIs encapsulate modules with specific purposes (e.g., cryptography, database access, logging) and abstract the implementation details. In this study, we focus on API-domain labels: high-level labels designating categories of APIs such as “UI,” “Security,” and “Test,” which may relate to the skills needed to work on the issues.

This paper extends our prior work [14], in which we conducted a case study with a single project to investigate the feasibility of automatically labeling issues with API-domain labels. After running the first predictions in the case study, we observed that the number of dataset rows dropped significantly due to the lack of information about linked issues and PRs. With this in mind, and to improve generalization, we looked for feasible ways to increase the datasets when a project is seriously affected by dataset size after discarding issues not linked with a PR. In addition, in industry projects it is sometimes impossible to access the source due to confidentiality. We therefore sought ways to keep predicting API-domain labels even when no training data is available, by transferring the learning. We believe the API-domain labels would be even more helpful if they could be applied in many open-source or industry projects regardless of their source code's dataset size or availability. We extend the work by (1) expanding the study to five projects with diverse programming languages, vocabularies (natural languages), and issue track systems (ITS), (2) adding the BERT technique to our approach, (3) extending the qualitative analysis, (4) exploring the ability to transfer learning across projects, and (5) evaluating the API-domain labels with developers who solved the issues.

We answer the following research questions:

RQ.1: How relevant are the API-domain labels to new contributors? RQ.2: To what extent can we automatically attribute API-domain labels to issues? RQ.2.1: To what extent can we automatically attribute API-domain labels to issues using data from the project? RQ.2.2: To what extent can we automatically attribute API-domain labels to issues using data from other projects? RQ.2.3: To what extent can we automatically attribute API-domain labels to issues using transfer learning? RQ.3: How well do the API-domain labels match the skills needed to solve an issue?

This paper studies the relevance of this labeling strategy to new contributors (RQ.1). We created models and evaluated their performance. Machine learning approaches usually train and test with data from the same project (RQ.2.1). However, when the existing data is not enough to create a prediction model with the expected performance, one may enlarge the dataset to include other projects (RQ.2.2). Moreover, when historical data for training is entirely absent in a target project, one can use a pre-trained dataset in the same domain (source project) to run predictions in the target project [15] (RQ.2.3), so we also conducted transfer learning studies. Finally, we studied developers' opinions about the predictions to determine whether the API-domain labels adequately indicate skills and help newcomers choose their tasks (RQ.3).

Our contributions include (1) how newcomers see the relevance of the API-domain labels; (2) a new semi-automated API classification process; (3) a mechanism to predict the skills needed for projects coded in diverse programming languages (C, C#, and Java), with issues in Portuguese and English; and (4) the validation of the API-domain labels with developers.
